title: The Rot Inside the Exam Room: How NTA Insiders Allegedly Sold NEET-UG 2026 Questions for Lakhs
excerpt: CBI arrests reveal a coaching-centre conspiracy that reached into the National Testing Agency itself — and 23 lakh students are paying the price
body:
The Central Bureau of Investigation's dragnet has now pulled in nine suspects across six cities in what is emerging as one of the most brazen breaches of examination security in India's history. On Saturday, the CBI arrested Manisha Gurunath Mandhare, a Pune-based senior botany lecturer who served on the National Testing Agency's own paper-setting committee for NEET-UG 2026. A day earlier, Professor P.V. Kulkarni, a veteran chemistry domain expert from Latur with years of access to NTA panels, was taken into custody. The charge: that they allegedly sold the very questions they had helped set.

## A System Compromised From Within

The modus operandi, as described by the CBI, is startling in its simplicity. In the last week of April 2026, Kulkarni and Mandhare allegedly convened special coaching sessions at their homes in Latur and Pune. Students — mobilised through an intermediary named Manisha Waghmare, arrested on May 14 — paid several lakh rupees each for the privilege of attending. During these sessions, the two lecturers allegedly dictated questions and answers from the NEET-UG biology and chemistry papers, making students note them down in notebooks and mark relevant passages in textbooks.

When 23 lakh candidates sat the exam on May 3, the questions "tallied exactly" with what had been shared in those sessions, the CBI said.

Mandhare, specifically, had "complete access" to both the Botany and Zoology question papers as an NTA-appointed expert. Her arrest in Delhi followed detailed questioning of Kulkarni, who has been described as a kingpin. The CBI has also conducted searches at six locations across the country, seizing laptops, mobile phones, bank statements, and documents. Forensic examination of the seized devices is under way.

## The Fallout: Cancellation, Chaos, and Heartbreak

The NTA said it first received information about "alleged malpractice" on the evening of May 7, four days after the exam. The inputs were escalated to central agencies the following morning. The exam was subsequently cancelled — a devastating blow for the nearly 23 lakh students who had registered.

A re-test has been announced for June 21, but the human cost is already mounting. Several suicide cases have been reported in the aftermath, as students who had prepared for months or years confronted the reality that the system designed to evaluate them had been rigged from the inside.

The examination had been conducted across 551 Indian cities and 14 overseas centres, making the logistical and emotional disruption enormous. For overseas aspirants — many of them children of NRIs who travelled to India specifically for the test — the cancellation introduces visa complications, travel costs, and the grinding uncertainty of a fresh preparation cycle.

## Context and Background: A Familiar Wound

This is not India's first encounter with examination fraud. In 2024, an earlier NEET paper leak scandal led to Supreme Court interventions and calls for structural reform. A parliamentary panel is currently reviewing NTA's processes, and a Supreme Court petition seeks to move NEET-UG to a computer-based format — a shift that would make physical paper leaks far harder to orchestrate.

Yet the 2026 case is qualitatively different because the breach came from inside the system. Previous scandals involved external actors — middlemen, exam-centre coordinators, dark-web networks. Here, the CBI's own statements point to NTA-appointed domain experts as the primary source. This is not a failure of perimeter security; it is a failure of institutional trust.

## What the Diaspora Is Watching

For the Indian diaspora, the NEET leak strikes at a particularly sensitive nerve. Medical education remains one of the most prestigious — and expensive — investments an Indian family can make. NRI parents routinely spend lakhs on coaching institutes, entrance-exam preparation, and flights to India for exam dates. The promise is that the process, however gruelling, is meritocratic.

That promise now looks hollow. With the CBI identifying at least nine accused across Delhi, Jaipur, Gurugram, Nasik, Pune, and Ahmedabad, and digital evidence still under analysis, the investigation appears far from over. Questions about how many students benefited from the leaked questions, whether other subjects were compromised, and whether similar breaches have occurred in past years remain unanswered.

## What's Next

The CBI has obtained a 14-day custody remand for Mandhare and a nine-day remand for Motegaonkar (the Latur coaching-centre director arrested earlier). The agency has said it is pursuing financial trails to identify the full scope of the conspiracy. The re-examination on June 21 will be conducted with enhanced security protocols, though the NTA has not yet detailed what those will entail. The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments on transitioning NEET-UG to a computer-based test in the coming weeks — a reform that, if enacted, could fundamentally alter how India's most consequential entrance exam is administered.
